# NYC Subway Simulator and Route Designer: A New Way to Visualize Public Transit

In the bustling metropolis of New York City, the subway system is a lifeline for millions. Yet, despite its critical importance, discussions around improving this intricate network often lack clarity and visual representation. Enter an innovative solution from a dedicated NYC resident who has developed a *Subway Simulator and Route Designer*—a tool designed to allow users to visualize and enhance subway operations without the complexities of construction or extensive planning.

## A Creative Endeavor

The creator of this simulator embarked on this ambitious project over a long weekend, inspired by the countless articles discussing potential improvements to subway services. The simulator allows users to spawn trains from their origin, make stops at various stations, and even slow down when approaching another train. Additionally, it grants users the ability to design custom routes by piecing together tracks, a feature that has sparked curiosity and conversation among users.

Users have noted the unique characteristics of the NYC subway, including its interlining and quadruple tracks, which offer numerous opportunities for enhancing system efficiency. As one commenter aptly pointed out, "In this simulator, you design services that run on existing tracks," reinforcing the notion that there is potential for improvement without the need for new routes.

## Community Engagement and Feedback

The response from the community has been overwhelmingly positive, with many users expressing excitement about the simulator's capabilities. One user, who contracts work to the MTA, noted their intention to share the simulator with the transit authority’s AI and innovation teams, highlighting its potential impact on real-world applications.

However, as with any new tool, feedback has also pointed out areas for improvement. Some users found the visual language of the simulator challenging to navigate and suggested incorporating colors aligned with actual subway lines to enhance usability. The creator acknowledged this feedback and has begun to implement changes, including color coding for the tracks and redesigning train visuals to improve clarity.

## Expanding Possibilities

The simulator's adaptability has also captured interest, especially its use of OpenStreetMap data. Users can easily modify the simulator for other cities by following straightforward steps to obtain infrastructure and service data. This opens up possibilities for urban planners and transit enthusiasts across the globe to explore and optimize their local transit systems.

Yet, while the simulator thrives on creativity and engagement, some users expressed frustration with limitations. For instance, attempts to create routes connecting Brooklyn to New Jersey highlighted the challenge of working within existing infrastructure. But this limitation also sparked conversations about the need for comprehensive public transport options, revealing the broader implications of the simulator beyond mere entertainment.

## The Future of Transit Visualization

This NYC Subway Simulator and Route Designer not only serves as a platform for fun but also acts as a catalyst for meaningful discussions about public transport efficiency and accessibility. As users brainstorm new routes and improvements, they engage with the complexities of urban transit in a way that is both informative and entertaining.

# From Photos to Positions: Prototyping VLM-Based Indoor Maps

In an age where technology continues to redefine our everyday experiences, a recent exploration into Vision Language Models (VLMs) has opened new doors for indoor navigation. A developer's personal project, born out of curiosity during a shopping trip, exemplifies how innovative thinking can yield practical solutions to common challenges.

## A Journey of Inspiration

The story begins with a reflective look back at the author's journey in tech, tracing their steps from high school to their current endeavors. It all started with a freelance project focused on indoor localization using Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) beacons. Fast forward to their university days, where they created an augmented reality (AR) app that helped students navigate their School of Computing. This foundation set the stage for the latest venture: harnessing VLM technologies to tackle the complexities of indoor mapping.

## The Concept Takes Shape

While visiting a shopping mall in Singapore in 2025, the author envisioned how VLMs could be employed to interpret maps similarly to a human's understanding. The initial goal was straightforward: to determine shop locations with a simple photograph. This idea quickly evolved into a weekend project that would lay the groundwork for a functional prototype.

In just a couple of days, the author successfully developed an annotation tool and a parsing tool, both of which facilitated the semantic processing of maps. A preprocessing function was incorporated as well, enabling the identification of visible shops from various corridor points through directional sampling. This inventive approach demonstrated the potential of merging VLMs with real-world applications.

## Bridging Visuals with Data

To bring the concept to life, the author created an API that utilized Google's Gemini API to query shop information based on images captured within the mall. This innovative API served as a bridge, matching visible shops against annotated locations, effectively creating an interactive map experience.

The results were promising. By leveraging just a photograph, the author was able to localize their position within the bustling mall, despite facing some challenges with ambiguities. The success of this prototype revealed the exciting possibilities that lie ahead, especially with the integration of video input and additional sensor data to enhance localization accuracy.

## Looking Ahead

This exploration is not merely a technical achievement; it represents a tantalizing glimpse into the future of indoor navigation. The author envisions a world where AR and robotics can seamlessly integrate with such technologies, transforming how we interact with our environments. However, they acknowledge that moving from proof-of-concept to a fully developed product will require time and further refinement.

Ultimately, this project highlights the innovative spirit that drives technology forward. While the author sees this endeavor as a fun experiment, the potential applications are vast and inviting. As VLMs continue to evolve, the fusion of visual processing and real-world navigation may soon become a reality, guiding us through complex indoor spaces with the ease of a simple snapshot.
